title: £2,000 cap on NI relief for salary-sacrificed pension contributions
registry_rule: The reform specification and the ASSUMPTION SWEEP for the Budget's largest NICs measure. This file stages NO value claims — IFS's assessment and the official costing belong to their originators (#86/#91) and are harvested in their own lane from primary documents, never copied from reporting into a spec.

baseline_evidence.uncapped_sentinel: inf, recorded as null in JSON — the parameter is uncapped before the measure bites
baseline_evidence.note: Answers the #99/#101 baseline-integrity question for this measure: CARRIED, with the dated step in the right place and the correct gov.uk references on the parameter.
baseline_evidence.checked_and_not_a_finding: The step is dated 2029-01-01 while the measure starts April 2029. Every parameter under gov.hmrc.national_insurance uses 01-01 — it is the module-wide convention, not an anomaly here. Recorded so a future reader does not re-raise it as a defect.

the_finding:
A DEFAULT PolicyEngine-UK score of this measure is NOT assumption-neutral, and the two assumptions point opposite ways. salary_sacrifice_broad_base_haircut_rate defaults to 0.0016 and is ON: it reduces employment income for ALL workers, not just sacrificers, on the reasoning that employers spread the added NI cost across the whole workforce. It is gated on the cap being finite, so it switches on exactly when the measure bites, and it cites a PolicyEngine research page as its methodology. Meanwhile employee_salary_sacrifice_reduction_rate defaults to 0 and is OFF: the response of employees actually reducing salary sacrifice once it is capped is not modelled by default.

That asymmetry is a PolicyEngine methodology choice, not HMRC's and not OBR's. Published without disclosure it would surface in a comparison as arithmetic disagreement. This is the #97 pattern (CGT's zero elasticity) but sharper, because there the default asserted no behaviour and here the default asserts some.

gov.contrib.behavioral_responses.salary_.applies_to: ALL workers' employment income, not only salary sacrificers
gov.contrib.behavioral_responses.salary_.gated_on: cap being finite (np.isinf(cap) -> 0), so it activates exactly at the measure
gov.contrib.behavioral_responses.salary_.provenance: PolicyEngine research methodology, cited on the variable itself

gov.contrib.behavioral_responses.employe.applies_to: employees reducing salary sacrifice in response to the cap

assumption_sweep.label: engine_default
assumption_sweep.source: The certified engine's own defaults. Publishing this leg still requires DISCLOSING the broad-base haircut, because unlike a static leg it asserts an incidence assumption.

assumption_sweep.label: no_behavioural_assumptions
assumption_sweep.source: Both assumptions switched off — the arithmetic-only leg. Asserts no behaviour, so it needs no citation, and it is the correct comparator for a static official costing.

comparison_rule: The published comparison must state which sweep leg it is. A leg with disclosure_required must name the broad-base haircut in the published note — a comparison that omits it reports a PolicyEngine incidence assumption as if it were arithmetic.
divergence_axes: broad_base_incidence: PE spreads employer NI cost across all workers by default; an external costing may not
employee_response: PE asserts none by default; an external costing may assume some
employer_ni_incidence: PE assumes full employee incidence (1.0)
not_yet_run: This PR specifies and resolves the reform; it computes no counterpart. UK counterpart compute runs through #51, which is not merged.
